title: How To Make Your Code Faster with Boolean Algebra
excerpt: It makes your code faster. Not in a theoretical or subtle way, in a "this exact line decides how much work your server does" way.

body.text: Why Every Programmer Should Learn Boolean Algebra

content.text: It makes your code faster. Not in a theoretical or subtle way, in a "this exact line decides how much work your server does" way.

A single Boolean expression can be the difference between code that returns in milliseconds and code that takes seconds. Look at these two conditions, they have the same functionality but one much faster.

data.explanation: Both conditions do identical work in the worst case. But && short-circuits: the moment the left side is false, the right side never runs. In Option A, the expensive function always executes first, whether or not the user is even logged in. In Option B, it only runs after you already know the user is logged in. Same logic, same result, different amount of work done to get there.

body.text: Boolean Algebra Isn't Just for Hardware

content.text: Most people stop thinking about Boolean algebra the day the digital logic final ends. That's a mistake, because it never actually left your code. Every
if
, every
while
, every SQL
WHERE
clause, every search filter your product runs is a Boolean expression evaluating true or false against real data.

The compiler doesn't know your intent, it only knows the expression you wrote. Two logically equivalent expressions can compile to wildly different amounts of runtime work, and the rules for which is which are exactly the rules of Boolean algebra: short-circuit evaluation, De Morgan's laws, distribution, factoring. You already used one of them in the last section without naming it.
The rest of this post is three of those rules, applied to code you'd actually write.
Short-circuit evaluation means
stops at the first false, and
stops at the first true. Whatever comes after that point never executes. Since you would rather short circuit from the less expensive function, the order matters.

data.explanation: isValidUser is almost certainly a boolean already sitting in memory. expensiveRegex has to walk the entire string. Put the cheap check first and the regex only runs for users who were going to pass anyway. Nothing about the result changes. Only the amount of work spent reaching it does.

body.text: Try it: order these from cheapest to most expensive

content.text: Use the arrows to reorder. These four checks are meant to be chained with && , and any one of them could be the one that fails. The cost numbers are illustrative, not a benchmark, chosen to be roughly the right order of magnitude relative to each other.

The second rule isn't about order, it's about redundant structure. Boolean algebra lets you factor a condition the same way you'd factor an equation, and the factored version usually costs less to evaluate and is easier for the next person to read.

data.prompt: Which of these is an equivalent, simpler rewrite?
data.explanation: This is the same distributive identity from the very first Karnaugh map tutorial: AB + AC = A(B + C). Here A is isAdmin, and it no longer gets checked twice. Beyond the runtime savings, which are real but small for a single boolean, the bigger win is maintenance: there is now exactly one place that says "you have to be an admin," instead of two places that could quietly drift apart.

content.text: Principle 1 showed the mechanism. Here's why it matters once you multiply it by real traffic. Say a permission check costs meaningfully more than a login check, and a request comes in from a user who isn't logged in.

data.explanationTemplate: In the bad order, expensivePermissionCheck() runs first, unconditionally, on every single request. In the good order, it only runs after isLoggedIn() already returned true. At {pct}% logged in, that's {saved} calls to an expensive function that never needed to happen.

content.text: WHERE indexed_col = ? AND slow_col LIKE ?

versus the same clauses reversed can be the difference between a query that hits an index and one that scans every row before it even gets to the cheap comparison. Query planners are smart, but they're not always smart enough to reorder around an expensive function call.

Cheap filters (category, price range, in-stock) should run before expensive ones (semantic similarity, fuzzy matching). Narrow the candidate set with boolean logic first, then spend the expensive computation only on what's left.

Axis-aligned bounding box checks are nearly free, compared to full physics collision resolution which can be expensive. Every collision system checks the cheap box first and only runs the expensive math for objects that were already close enough to plausibly collide. These are the kinds of optimizations which can give huge returns in performance from something as simple as changing the order of an if statement or prioritizing less expensive tasks.

data.prompt: Reorder it in your head, then check your answer.
data.explanation: userExists, hasPermission, and hasSubscription read like plain booleans, values already sitting in memory or a cheap lookup, not function calls that do real work. expensiveValidation(data) is named like the one thing here that actually costs something. Move it last, and it only runs for requests that already cleared every cheap gate.

data.title: Boolean Algebra for Programmers: Recap
data.passMessage: Solid, you've internalized the short-circuit habit.
data.failMessage: Worth skimming the three principles above again.

questions.prompt: Why does putting isLoggedIn() before expensivePermissionCheck() help?

options.label: && short-circuits, so the expensive call never runs once the cheap one is false
JavaScript automatically reorders conditions for you
It changes the result of the expression

questions.explanation: Short-circuiting is the whole mechanism: the moment the left side of && is false, the right side never executes, regardless of order elsewhere in the file.

questions.prompt: isAdmin && canEdit || isAdmin && canDelete simplifies to which factored form?
questions.explanation: Same distributive identity as the Karnaugh map tutorials: AB + AC = A(B + C). isAdmin is now checked exactly once.

questions.prompt: In a WHERE clause, why can column order matter for performance?

options.label: Query planners are always smart enough to reorder around it, so it never matters
An indexed, cheap comparison first can avoid a full scan before an expensive comparison runs
SQL evaluates every clause in alphabetical order

questions.explanation: Query planners are smart, but not always smart enough to reorder around an expensive function call, so putting the indexed/cheap condition first still matters in practice.

content.text: - Put cheap conditions first, expensive ones last. Short-circuiting does the rest.
- Factor repeated logic instead of duplicating it. Less work, and one source of truth.
- Remove evaluations you don't need before you optimize the ones you do.
- You can even do a simpler check before doing an expensive one to sift unlikely candidates, kind of like what we discussed with the hitboxes earlier.
